profiles.meeting_scenario: A national law firm's labor-and-employment group is holding a brainstorming meeting to shape a client-facing webinar and follow-up advisory for employer clients on "proxy discrimination" risks in AI-enabled HR systems. The immediate trigger is that several existing clients have asked whether removing race, sex, disability, and health-status fields from recruiting and workforce analytics tools is enough to reduce liability. The agenda is to generate practical framing, example use cases, and a short menu of compliance strategies the firm can present without committing to a full formal opinion. The expected outcome is a rough outline for the webinar and a shortlist of service offerings the firm could package, such as a model review, a fairness audit, or governance guidance for vendors and internal HR teams.

members.name: Dana Mercer
members.expertise: Title VII disparate impact, ADA and benefits discrimination, employment litigation strategy, EEOC investigations
members.background: Former EEOC trial attorney who now advises large employers on hiring assessments, workforce policies, and defensible documentation practices.
members.private_state: Wants the webinar to stay tightly anchored to doctrines clients already recognize, so the firm sounds practical rather than academic; also wants any proposed service to be easy for employment clients to buy quickly.
hidden_assumptions: When lawyers say "proxy discrimination," they usually mean a plaintiff can point to a facially neutral employment input that functions as a stand-in for a protected trait in a way a court would recognize under existing disparate-impact doctrine.

In an employment-AI discussion, the natural universe is pre-employment screening, promotion scoring, and termination-risk tools, not adjacent systems like benefits administration or wellness analytics.
Shorthand references to "the New York City framework" usually center on the independent bias-audit concept from Local Law 144, because that is the part employment clients ask about most.

A "fairness audit" for legal-risk purposes normally means reviewing outcome disparities using existing demographic data and validation materials, not technically re-engineering the model or searching for latent proxies before deployment.

members.name: Ravi Sethi
members.expertise: AI governance, algorithmic accountability, privacy-by-design, vendor contracting, emerging state and local AI regulation
members.background: Former product counsel at an HR technology vendor who now advises employers and software suppliers on automated decision systems and data governance.
members.private_state: Wants to position the firm as ahead of the market by offering a broader AI-governance package, not just employment-defense talking points; also wants the discussion to capture product-design and vendor-management angles.
hidden_assumptions: Proxy discrimination includes unintentional but rational substitution, even where doctrine is unsettled, because the practical compliance problem starts before a fully justiciable claim is framed.

In the employment setting, proxy-risk analysis naturally includes not only hiring and promotion tools but also scheduling, productivity monitoring, leave triage, wellness programs, and benefits-related analytics if they affect conditions of employment.
When practitioners mention "the New York City framework," they usually mean the combined package of audit, notice, publication, and candidate-rights obligations that clients operationalize together.

A "fairness audit" is primarily a pre-deployment technical exercise that probes for hidden proxies and model behavior, often with vendor test environments and feature-level analysis rather than only post hoc legal disparity review.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the webinar should explain "proxy discrimination" clearly for clients.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a relatively bounded legal category tied to recognizable disparate-impact or proxy-use theories that can be articulated in current employment doctrine.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the broader governance problem of models finding substitutes for protected traits whenever those traits are predictive, even if a clean present-day cause of action is not yet settled.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are comfortable using the same article-driven phrase and both want to help clients avoid risk, so the conversation can proceed smoothly without either noticing that one is framing a doctrinal label and the other a wider compliance concept.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in the "employment context"
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both talk about covering AI risks in the "employment context" or for "employer clients."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the discussion covers hiring, promotion, performance ranking, and termination-related decision tools.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes it also includes workforce scheduling, productivity monitoring, leave triage, wellness scoring, and benefits-adjacent analytics that influence employees' opportunities or conditions.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Neither interpretation sounds controversial because both are plausibly employment-related, and in a brainstorming meeting broad labels like "employer use cases" feel sufficient without anyone listing the boundaries explicitly.

misalignment_points.topic: What "the New York City framework" refers to
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they can "lean on the New York City framework" as a concrete example for clients.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking specifically of New York City Local Law 144's independent bias-audit requirement for automated employment decision tools.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the broader operational package clients associate with New York City: bias audit, notice to candidates, publication of audit summaries, and accommodation or alternative-selection-process expectations discussed in the rules and agency guidance.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds like efficient expert shorthand, and each person can build on it without contradiction because the narrower audit requirement and the broader compliance bundle overlap enough to create false consensus.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that one service offering could be a "fairness audit" for client systems.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a legally oriented review of existing model outputs, adverse-impact ratios, validation memos, and demographic outcome tables using the employer's current records.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a pre-deployment or parallel technical assessment that stress-tests the model for hidden proxies through feature review, sandbox testing, and vendor-side analysis before relying on production outcomes.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: A fairness audit is commonly described at a high level in multidisciplinary teams, and both procedures plausibly fit under the same label, so neither speaker feels the need to specify the mechanics during an initial idea-generation meeting.

turns.inner_thought: Clients keep asking the same narrow question: if they strip out race, sex, disability, or health-status fields from a hiring or promotion tool, are they safe? I want the webinar to answer that in a way that maps onto current employment doctrine, especially disparate impact and recognizable proxy-use theories, not drift into abstract ethics. And it needs to stay centered on the core employment decision tools clients already budget for.
turns.utterance: I keep getting the version of the question that goes, "If we deleted the protected-class fields, aren't we done?" So I think there's a real opportunity for a short client webinar on proxy discrimination in AI tools used by employer clients. We can make it practical and answer the question they're already asking.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, that's exactly the opening, but I want to broaden it beyond litigable doctrines. The real governance problem is that systems can infer protected traits from other inputs across the whole employment context—recruiting, yes, but also scheduling, monitoring, leave, wellness, benefits-adjacent analytics. This is a chance to position us as ahead of the market, not just reactive defense counsel.
turns.utterance: I agree. The useful message for clients is that removing obvious fields doesn't necessarily solve proxy discrimination, because systems can still recreate the same risk across the employment context if the team thinks it has sanitized the data. That lands with both legal and operational audiences.

turns.inner_thought: Let's keep this grounded in familiar hiring and promotion fact patterns so employers instantly recognize the doctrine and don't hear us as theorizing. If we anchor in screening, promotion scoring, and similar decisions, the path from problem to legal framework is straightforward and easy to sell as a follow-up review.
turns.utterance: For the examples, I'd start with the familiar employment context and keep the framing close to what clients already know. If we show proxy discrimination through the kinds of tools they already associate with employment law risk, they'll be able to map it onto doctrines they recognize instead of hearing it as something academic.

turns.inner_thought: I don't want the audience to think this is only about recruiting. Some of the most interesting client demand is around scheduling engines, attendance-risk models, productivity tools, leave triage, and wellness scoring. Those are all part of the employment context in practice, and they open the door to governance and vendor-management work.
turns.utterance: That makes sense, and I think we can still make the employment context feel broader by using a few different illustrations. Scheduling, attendance-risk, and wellness-related analytics would resonate too, because employer clients are already encountering those tools and asking similar questions about proxy discrimination.

turns.inner_thought: Fine, a few extra illustrations are okay as long as we don't lose the center of gravity. For a concrete anchor, I should invoke New York City, because clients immediately think of the audit requirement under Local Law 144. That's the clearest shorthand and the most market-recognized reference point.
turns.utterance: To keep the session grounded, we can lean on the New York City framework as the clearest concrete example employers already recognize. It gives us something tangible without turning the webinar into a fifty-state survey.

turns.inner_thought: Good. When I say the New York City framework, I mean the whole operational package clients actually have to implement: audit, notice, publication, and related candidate-facing processes. That's exactly the kind of bridge from doctrine to governance that I want to emphasize.
turns.utterance: Yes, and the nice thing about leaning on the New York City framework is that it feels real to compliance teams. We can talk about the audit piece, publication, notice, and the related operational expectations in one package so clients see how this works in practice.

turns.inner_thought: Now we're getting to a service offering. A fairness audit should be something employment clients can buy quickly: review current outcomes, adverse impact, existing validation materials, and documentation gaps. No need to promise model engineering or deep technical probing. Keep it legally legible and scoped.
turns.utterance: On the follow-up advisory side, one practical package could be a fairness audit for an existing system. We could review outcome disparities, the supporting validation materials, and the core documentation so the client has a clearer view of where the risk sits.

turns.inner_thought: That's useful, but I also want fairness audit to mean something more robust and forward-looking: pre-deployment testing in a vendor sandbox, feature behavior review, and checking for hidden proxies before the tool goes live. If I can fold that in under the same label, we can create a broader AI-governance package without having to relitigate terminology.
turns.utterance: I like that, and I think a fairness audit also gives us room to help before rollout, not just after the fact. If we can work with the client and the vendor in a test environment and examine how the system behaves, that makes the offering stronger and more forward-looking.

turns.inner_thought: I should end with a checklist clients can recognize immediately: approved inputs, business rationale, validation, statistical checks. That's concrete, doctrinally familiar, and easy to convert into a short advisory. When I say isolate non-suspect predictive power, I mean something that can be defended with existing records, not an open-ended technical redesign exercise.
turns.utterance: For the webinar close, I'd give them a short menu of strategies: approved-variable lists, documentation of business rationale, and statistical checks that help show what the system is actually relying on. That way proxy discrimination doesn't sound mysterious; it sounds like a manageable compliance and documentation problem.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. I'll package this as enterprise governance for employer AI systems so we can pull in legal, product, procurement, and HR stakeholders. Dana thinks we're aligned on a bounded employment-law offering, and that's fine for now; I can draft an outline broad enough to preserve the vendor-management and design angles under the same shared language.
turns.utterance: That works well. I think the overall takeaway can be framed as enterprise governance for employer AI systems, with proxy discrimination as the thread that ties the webinar together. I'm happy to draft a first outline that covers the examples, the New York City framework, and the service menu we just discussed.
